questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with several months of fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. Laboratory studies show a serum TSH of 24 microunits/mL (elevated) and a low free T4. Which node of the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis is most likely disrupted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic TRH-secreting neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary thyrotrophs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thyroid follicular cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peripheral T4-to-T3 converting tissue

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nuclear thyroid hormone receptors in target cells

explanation.summary: High TSH with low thyroid hormone localizes the lesion to the thyroid gland itself (primary hypothyroidism).
explanation.whyCorrect: When the thyroid cannot make T3/T4, the negative feedback that normally suppresses TRH and TSH is lost, so the intact hypothalamus and pituitary drive TSH upward while thyroid hormone stays low. This high-TSH/low-T4 fingerprint is the signature of failure at the peripheral gland. Her fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance are the effector-output consequences of reduced metabolic rate and thermogenesis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of hypothalamic TRH would lower the drive to the pituitary, producing low TSH along with low T3/T4.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pituitary failure removes the TSH signal, so TSH and thyroid hormone fall together rather than diverging.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired peripheral conversion lowers T3 while T4 is maintained and would not markedly raise TSH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptor-level resistance blunts downstream effect while circulating thyroid hormone stays normal or high, not low.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man is evaluated for fatigue and cold intolerance. Serum TSH is low and free T4 is low. Exogenous TRH is administered, and serum TSH remains flat over the next hour. Which node is most likely disrupted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic TRH secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary TSH secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thyroid follicular cell hormone synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: TSH receptors on the thyroid gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: Peripheral conversion of T4 to T3

explanation.summary: Low TSH with low T4 and no TSH response to exogenous TRH localizes the failure to the pituitary thyrotroph.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary hypothyroidism arises when the pituitary cannot generate the TSH signal, leaving the thyroid unstimulated and both hormones low. Supplying TRH from outside tests whether the pituitary can respond; a flat TSH shows the defect is in the pituitary itself rather than upstream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A hypothalamic lesion also gives low TSH and low T4, but the pituitary is intact, so exogenous TRH would raise TSH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Failure of the gland removes feedback inhibition and drives TSH high, the opposite of the pattern shown.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of thyroid TSH receptors leaves the pituitary free to secrete, so TSH would be elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A conversion defect lowers T3 selectively and does not suppress TSH secretion.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has low serum TSH and low free T4. After exogenous TRH is given, serum TSH rises briskly. Which node is most likely disrupted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic TRH secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary TSH secretion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Thyroid follicular cell hormone synthesis

choices.label: D
choices.text: TSH receptors on the thyroid gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nuclear thyroid hormone receptors in target tissue

explanation.summary: A pituitary that responds normally to exogenous TRH places the defect one level higher, in the hypothalamus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The hypothalamus is the integrating center that secretes TRH into the portal system to drive pituitary thyrotrophs. If it fails, TRH is absent, so TSH and thyroid hormone are both low; the thyrotrophs themselves are intact, so replacing TRH from outside restores the TSH rise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A failed pituitary cannot respond to TRH, so TSH would remain flat after the stimulus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gland failure produces high TSH with low thyroid hormone because feedback inhibition is lost.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of thyroid TSH receptors leaves pituitary output unopposed, so TSH would be high.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Target-cell receptor loss leaves circulating hormone normal or high rather than low.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has palpitations, heat intolerance, and weight loss. Serum TSH is elevated and free T4 and T3 are both elevated. MRI shows a sellar mass. Which mechanism best explains this hormone pattern?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loss of thyroid hormone output that removes feedback inhibition

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absent pituitary signal leaving the thyroid unstimulated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reduced target-cell receptor sensitivity to thyroid hormone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Autonomous TSH secretion that bypasses negative feedback

choices.label: E
choices.text: Failure of the hypothalamus to release its tropic hormone

explanation.summary: High TSH together with high T3/T4 indicates a tumor secreting TSH independently of the feedback loop.
explanation.whyCorrect: Normally rising T3/T4 would suppress TSH, so elevated TSH in the face of elevated thyroid hormone can only occur if the source of TSH ignores the feedback signal. A TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma produces the hormone autonomously, driving continued thyroid stimulation and thyrotoxic symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of gland output raises TSH but leaves T3/T4 low, not elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An absent pituitary signal drives TSH and T3/T4 down together.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptor resistance blunts the tissue response and does not by itself raise circulating T3/T4 with hyperthyroid symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A hypothalamic lesion lowers TRH, so TSH and thyroid hormone both fall.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism asks why her levothyroxine is a daily tablet while her insulin must be injected. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Levothyroxine is hydrophilic and therefore absorbed across the gut

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin is a peptide and must be injected to preserve its structure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin acts on nuclear receptors that require slow sustained delivery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Levothyroxine is a peptide that resists degradation in the stomach

choices.label: E
choices.text: Insulin is a steroid that is inactivated by hepatic first-pass metabolism

explanation.summary: Route of administration follows hormone class: peptides must be given parenterally, while lipophilic steroid and thyroid hormones can be taken orally.
explanation.whyCorrect: Insulin is a hydrophilic peptide hormone that requires injection to preserve structure and function, after which it acts through surface receptor cascades within minutes. Thyroid hormone is lipophilic, survives oral administration, and works by altering gene expression over hours to days, which is why replacement is titrated gradually.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thyroid hormones are lipophilic, not hydrophilic; that lipid solubility is what permits oral dosing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin binds cell-surface receptors coupled to second messengers, not nuclear receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Levothyroxine is an iodinated amine derivative, not a peptide hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin is a peptide synthesized as a prohormone, not a cholesterol-derived steroid.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with an asthma exacerbation receives inhaled albuterol and oral prednisone. His wheezing improves within minutes, but the anti-inflammatory benefit of the prednisone is not apparent for many hours. Which property of steroid hormones best explains this delay?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They activate membrane G-protein-coupled receptors and second messengers

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are secreted as prohormones requiring cleavage before activity

choices.label: C
choices.text: They must be delivered through a portal circulation to reach targets

choices.label: D
choices.text: They require peripheral deiodination before binding their receptor

choices.label: E
choices.text: They act as ligand-activated transcription factors altering gene expression

explanation.summary: Lipophilic steroid hormones signal through intracellular nuclear receptors, so their effects unfold over hours to days.
explanation.whyCorrect: Steroids are synthesized from cholesterol and cross the membrane to bind intracellular ligand-activated transcription factors. Because the effector output is a change in gene expression rather than a preexisting enzyme cascade, the physiological response is delayed, which is exactly why corticosteroid onset lags behind a fast surface-receptor drug.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Membrane receptor cascades are the fast pathway used by peptides and catecholamines, producing effects within minutes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prohormone processing characterizes peptide hormone synthesis, not steroid synthesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal delivery describes the hypothalamic-pituitary link, not the reason corticosteroids act slowly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Deiodination applies to thyroid hormone conversion, not to cholesterol-derived steroids.

questions.stem: In a simple endocrine reflex, an endocrine cell directly detects a fall in a circulating substrate and secretes its hormone in response without any input from the central nervous system. Which statement about the control elements of this pathway is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hypothalamus serves as the integrating center for the reflex

choices.label: B
choices.text: The secreted hormone functions as the sensor for the reflex

choices.label: C
choices.text: The endocrine cell serves as both the sensor and the integrating center

choices.label: D
choices.text: The target tissue serves as the integrating center for the reflex

choices.label: E
choices.text: The pathway operates without any feedback signal at all

explanation.summary: In simple endocrine reflexes the same endocrine cell both detects the change and compares it against the set point.
explanation.whyCorrect: The sensor detects the stimulus and the integrating center compares input to a set point; these are usually separate structures, but in a simple endocrine reflex an endocrine cell monitoring a circulating substrate performs both roles. The four control elements (stimulus, sensor, integrating center, feedback signal) are still present, only collapsed into fewer structures.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The hypothalamus is the integrating center in neuroendocrine and multi-tiered axes, not in a reflex with no CNS input.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The hormone is a molecular signaling component that carries the message, not the structure that detects change.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The target tissue generates the effector output; it does not compare input against a set point.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hormone's effect on the substrate still loops back as the feedback signal that closes the circuit.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old man with obesity has a fasting plasma glucose of 168 mg/dL and a markedly elevated fasting serum insulin concentration. Which type of pathway disruption best accounts for these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reduced target-cell receptor sensitivity with compensatory hormone secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Destruction of the hormone-secreting cells with intact target receptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autonomous hormone secretion from a tumor that bypasses feedback

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the integrating center to release its tropic hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absent second messengers because the hormone never reaches circulation

explanation.summary: High circulating hormone with a deficient downstream effect is the fingerprint of receptor-level disruption.
explanation.whyCorrect: When receptors are downregulated or mutated, effector output falls even though hormone levels are normal or high; the pathway senses the inadequate response and secretes more hormone. In type 2 diabetes, reduced insulin receptor sensitivity produces compensatory hyperinsulinemia while glucose uptake remains impaired.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Loss of the secreting cells would produce low, not markedly elevated, circulating insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autonomous secretion from a tumor would drive glucose down rather than leave it elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Insulin release is a simple endocrine reflex from the pancreas, and a missing tropic signal would lower insulin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Insulin is clearly reaching the circulation here, since its measured concentration is high.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman is undergoing ovulation monitoring. Mid-cycle, her serum estradiol rises steadily and is followed by an abrupt surge in luteinizing hormone and then ovulation. Which regulatory mechanism does this sequence illustrate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Negative feedback, in which output suppresses the upstream drive

choices.label: B
choices.text: Receptor downregulation, in which target cells lose responsiveness

choices.label: C
choices.text: Set-point resetting, in which the integrating center is bypassed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive feedback, in which output amplifies the signal that produced it

choices.label: E
choices.text: Signal amplification, in which each tier magnifies the tier above

explanation.summary: The mid-cycle LH surge is the classic example of positive feedback in an endocrine axis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Positive feedback amplifies rather than suppresses the original signal, so rising estrogen stimulates further LH release until ovulation is triggered. It is inherently unstable and therefore reserved for rapid, all-or-nothing events rather than sustained homeostatic control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Negative feedback would have rising estrogen shut LH secretion down, not drive it to surge.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Receptor downregulation reduces the response to a hormone; here responsiveness is escalating.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hypothalamic-pituitary integrating center is participating in this response, not being bypassed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Amplification across tiers describes how a small signal is magnified, but it does not explain the self-reinforcing rise.

questions.stem: A healthy adult moves into a cold environment, and circulating thyroid hormone falls below its set point. Which sequence correctly orders the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis from stimulus to effector output?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Low T3/T4, then TSH, then TRH, then T3/T4, then metabolic effects

choices.label: B
choices.text: Low T3/T4, then TRH, then TSH, then T3/T4, then metabolic effects

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low T3/T4, then TSH, then T3/T4, then metabolic effects, then TRH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low T3/T4, then TRH, then metabolic effects, then TSH, then T3/T4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Low T3/T4, then T3/T4, then TRH, then TSH, then metabolic effects

explanation.summary: The HPT axis runs top down: hypothalamus, then anterior pituitary, then thyroid, then target tissue.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hypothalamic neurons sense the low thyroid hormone and secrete TRH into the portal system; TRH binds G-protein-coupled receptors on pituitary thyrotrophs to release TSH; TSH stimulates thyroid follicular cells to make T4 and T3; T3 then binds nuclear receptors in target cells to change gene expression and metabolic rate.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This places pituitary TSH before hypothalamic TRH, reversing the anatomic hierarchy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This omits the hypothalamic step from the efferent limb and appends TRH after the response.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Metabolic effects cannot precede the secretion of the hormone that produces them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thyroid hormone cannot rise before the tropic signals that stimulate its synthesis.

questions.stem: A hormone is synthesized from the amino acid tyrosine and exerts its effects by entering the nucleus of target cells and binding a transcription factor receptor. Which hormone has these properties?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Follicle-stimulating hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroxine

explanation.summary: Thyroid hormones are the amine-derived hormones that are lipophilic and act on nuclear receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Amine hormones are built from tyrosine, tryptophan, or histidine, and most of them are hydrophilic and use membrane receptors. Thyroid hormones are the exception: they are lipophilic amine derivatives whose receptors are nuclear transcription factors, so T3 enters the nucleus and modulates gene expression governing metabolism, thermogenesis, and cardiac function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epinephrine is also tyrosine-derived but is hydrophilic and signals through cell membrane receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol acts on an intracellular receptor but is synthesized from cholesterol rather than an amino acid.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Insulin is a peptide made as a prohormone and binds a cell-surface receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Follicle-stimulating hormone is a protein hormone acting at membrane receptors on target cells.

questions.stem: In the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis, an extremely small quantity of TRH delivered through the portal system produces a much larger mass of circulating thyroid hormone and a body-wide change in metabolic rate. Which property of multi-tiered endocrine axes best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each anatomical level dampens the signal to protect the target tissue

choices.label: B
choices.text: The hypothalamus releases its hormone directly into systemic circulation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each anatomical level amplifies the signal received from the level above

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tropic hormones act on adjacent cells by paracrine diffusion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Positive feedback at each tier sustains the response once initiated

explanation.summary: Amplification at every tier lets a small hypothalamic input drive a large, coordinated peripheral response.
explanation.whyCorrect: In a multi-tiered axis the hypothalamus signals the anterior pituitary, which signals a peripheral gland, which acts on target tissue, and each transition magnifies the signal from the level above. That is why tiny hypothalamic outputs produce system-wide effects, and why each level is also a discrete point of regulation and of potential disruption.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dampening at each step would make the axis progressively less effective, the opposite of what occurs.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Hypothalamic releasing hormones travel through the hypothalamic-pituitary portal system, not the systemic circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Endocrine pathways are defined by delivery through circulation to distant targets rather than paracrine diffusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The HPT axis is governed by negative feedback; rising T3/T4 suppresses TRH and TSH.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman reports that she has been bumping into objects at the edges of her vision for several months. Formal testing shows loss of the outer visual fields in both eyes. MRI demonstrates a mass filling and expanding the sella turcica. Compression of which structure best explains her visual findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dorsum sellae, which lies immediately superior to the gland

choices.label: B
choices.text: Infundibulum, which lies immediately inferior to the gland

choices.label: C
choices.text: Optic chiasm, which lies immediately superior to the gland

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cavernous sinus, which lies immediately superior to the gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sphenoid sinus, which lies immediately superior to the gland

explanation.summary: The optic chiasm sits directly above the pituitary, so a growing sellar mass compresses it and takes out peripheral vision.
explanation.whyCorrect: The chiasm is the crossing point of the left and right optic nerves and lies just superior to the pituitary gland. An enlarging gland pushes upward out of the hypophyseal fossa and presses on the chiasm, producing bilateral loss of the peripheral visual fields. This superior relationship is one of the key reasons sellar imaging is interpreted with the surrounding structures in mind.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The dorsum sellae is the bony wall posterior to the gland and is not a visual pathway structure.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The infundibulum runs superiorly from the gland to the hypothalamus, not inferiorly, and it carries no visual fibers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cavernous sinuses lie lateral to the pituitary on each side, not above it, and compression there affects cranial nerves rather than vision fields.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The sphenoid sinus lies inferior to the gland and forms the floor of the sella turcica.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with a pituitary tumor that has extended laterally develops horizontal double vision and cannot abduct the right eye. Pupillary responses, eye elevation, and facial sensation are intact. Which feature best explains why this cranial nerve was affected before the others?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It runs freely within the cavernous sinus, while the others sit embedded in the lateral wall

choices.label: B
choices.text: It runs embedded in the medial wall of the cavernous sinus, while the others run freely

choices.label: C
choices.text: It passes through the optic canal directly above the pituitary, while the others pass laterally

choices.label: D
choices.text: It crosses the floor of the sella turcica within the sphenoid sinus, while the others stay above

choices.label: E
choices.text: It travels in the carotid sheath lateral to the cavernous sinus, while the others travel inside

explanation.summary: CN VI courses freely inside the cavernous sinus next to the internal carotid artery, making it the first nerve hit by lateral pituitary extension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within the cavernous sinus, the abducens nerve is suspended in the sinus itself alongside the internal carotid artery and has no bony or dural cushion. Cranial nerves III, IV, V1, and V2 are embedded within the lateral wall of the sinus, where they are partially protected. Consequently, a mass expanding into the cavernous sinus typically produces an isolated lateral rectus palsy before other cranial nerve deficits appear.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The nerve is not embedded in a medial wall; it is the one nerve that runs unprotected within the sinus lumen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The optic canal transmits the optic nerve, and compression there would cause visual loss rather than an abduction deficit.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No cranial nerve to the extraocular muscles runs through the sphenoid sinus beneath the sellar floor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The carotid sheath is a neck structure containing the common carotid artery, internal jugular vein, and vagus nerve.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with a hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma is scheduled for resection. The neurosurgeon plans an approach through the nasal cavity that avoids retracting the brain. Which structure must the surgeon traverse to reach the gland?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Frontal sinus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maxillary sinus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Third ventricle

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sphenoid sinus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cavernous sinus

explanation.summary: Transsphenoidal surgery reaches the pituitary through the nasal cavity and the sphenoid sinus, which forms the floor of the sella.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pituitary sits in the hypophyseal fossa directly above the sphenoid sinus, and that sinus communicates with the nasal cavity. Passing through it gives a direct midline corridor to the gland while sparing the brain from retraction. This is why the transsphenoidal route is the most common approach for pituitary surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The frontal sinus lies well above and anterior to the sella and is not on the route to the pituitary.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The maxillary sinus sits lateral and inferior within the face and does not border the hypophyseal fossa.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The third ventricle lies superior to the hypothalamus, and entering it would require the very brain retraction this approach avoids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The cavernous sinuses flank the gland laterally and are deliberately avoided because of the carotid artery and cranial nerves within them.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman has massive postpartum hemorrhage requiring transfusion. Over the following weeks she is unable to breastfeed and develops fatigue and amenorrhea. Which mechanism best accounts for her endocrine failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Occlusion of the internal carotid artery proximal to both hypophyseal branches

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ischemic necrosis of the adenohypophysis, which depends on portal venous perfusion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ischemic necrosis of the neurohypophysis, which depends on portal venous perfusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thrombosis of the cavernous sinus obstructing venous outflow from the gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: Compression of the infundibulum interrupting axonal transport from the hypothalamus

explanation.summary: The anterior pituitary is perfused by the low-pressure hypophyseal portal system, which makes it uniquely vulnerable to hemorrhagic hypotension.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rather than receiving a direct arterial supply, the anterior pituitary is fed by portal veins descending from a hypothalamic capillary plexus through the infundibulum. When perfusion pressure falls during severe postpartum hemorrhage, this arrangement leaves the adenohypophysis prone to ischemic necrosis, the lesion of Sheehan syndrome. Loss of anterior lobe hormones explains her failed lactation, fatigue, and amenorrhea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carotid occlusion would produce major cerebral ischemia rather than isolated anterior pituitary failure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The posterior lobe is supplied directly by the inferior hypophyseal arteries, so it is not the portal-dependent tissue at risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cavernous sinus thrombosis obstructs venous return and involves the nerves in the sinus rather than causing anterior lobe hormone loss after hemorrhage.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stalk compression is a mass effect and does not follow from obstetric blood loss.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman is found on examination to have a smooth anterior neck mass that rises when she is asked to swallow. Which anatomic feature best explains this movement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gland is suspended from the hyoid bone by the infrahyoid muscles

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gland lies within the carotid sheath and moves with the great vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gland is tethered posteriorly to the wall of the cervical esophagus

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gland is embedded within the fibers of the cricothyroid membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gland is anchored by its fibrous capsule to the larynx and trachea

explanation.summary: The thyroid moves with swallowing because its capsule fixes it to the larynx and trachea, which elevate during deglutition.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thyroid gland is enclosed by a fibrous capsule and firmly attached to the laryngeal and tracheal cartilages it wraps around. When the larynx and trachea rise during swallowing, the gland and any mass within it rise with them. Clinicians use this sign at the bedside to identify a neck mass as thyroid in origin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The infrahyoid muscles lie anterior to the gland as strap muscles and do not suspend it from the hyoid.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The carotid sheath with the common carotid artery and internal jugular vein lies lateral to the thyroid, not around it.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The esophagus lies posterior to the trachea and is not the structure that fixes the gland in place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The cricothyroid membrane spans between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages and does not enclose glandular tissue.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man undergoes total thyroidectomy for a large goiter. On the first postoperative day his voice is markedly hoarse, and laryngoscopy shows impaired vocal cord mobility. Injury to which nerve is most likely?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glossopharyngeal nerve

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spinal accessory nerve

choices.label: C
choices.text: Recurrent laryngeal nerve

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phrenic nerve

choices.label: E
choices.text: Hypoglossal nerve

explanation.summary: The recurrent laryngeal nerves run posterolateral to the thyroid and supply most intrinsic laryngeal muscles, so thyroid surgery risks hoarseness and cord paralysis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The left and right recurrent laryngeal nerves course posterolaterally along the thyroid gland, immediately adjacent to the operative field in thyroidectomy. Because they innervate most of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx, injury produces hoarseness, voice change, or vocal cord paralysis. Their proximity to the gland is the reason they are carefully identified during neck surgery.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The glossopharyngeal nerve serves pharyngeal sensation and the stylopharyngeus, not the vocal cords.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The spinal accessory nerve innervates the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius in the posterior triangle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The phrenic nerve descends on the anterior scalene to the diaphragm, and injury causes hemidiaphragm paralysis rather than hoarseness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hypoglossal nerve supplies the tongue muscles and is well above the thyroid bed.

questions.stem: Two days after a difficult thyroidectomy, a 62-year-old woman develops perioral tingling and carpal spasm, and serum calcium is low. The surgeon suspects that the blood supply to the small glands on the posterior thyroid surface was disrupted. Which vessels were most likely compromised?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inferior phrenic arteries

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inferior thyroid arteries

choices.label: C
choices.text: Superior thyroid arteries

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thyroid ima artery

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superior hypophyseal arteries

explanation.summary: The parathyroid glands are supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid arteries, so their disruption during thyroid surgery causes postoperative hypocalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inferior thyroid arteries, branches of the thyrocervical trunks, supply the posterior and inferior thyroid as well as the parathyroid glands embedded on that posterior surface. This shared circulation is why parathyroid function can fail when these vessels are ligated or injured during thyroidectomy. Loss of parathyroid hormone then drops serum calcium, producing tetany.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The inferior phrenic arteries give rise to the superior adrenal arteries in the abdomen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The superior thyroid arteries, from the external carotids, supply the superior and anterior thyroid rather than the parathyroids.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The thyroid ima artery is an inconstant vessel that supplies the isthmus when present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The superior hypophyseal arteries supply the pituitary gland at the base of the brain.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with resistant hypertension undergoes adrenal venous sampling to localize excess aldosterone production. To sample the left adrenal gland, the interventional radiologist advances the catheter from the inferior vena cava into which vessel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Left hepatic vein

choices.label: B
choices.text: Left inferior phrenic artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Splenic vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Left brachiocephalic vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Left renal vein

explanation.summary: Each adrenal drains through a single vein: the right empties into the inferior vena cava, the left into the left renal vein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although each adrenal gland receives arterial blood from three sources, venous blood from cortex and medulla converges into one adrenal vein. On the left, that vein drains into the left renal vein, so a catheter in the inferior vena cava must be advanced into the left renal vein to reach it. On the right, the adrenal vein enters the inferior vena cava directly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The adrenal veins do not drain into hepatic veins on either side.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The inferior phrenic artery gives off superior adrenal arteries and carries blood toward, not away from, the gland.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The splenic vein drains the pancreas and spleen into the portal venous system.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The brachiocephalic veins receive the inferior thyroid veins in the thorax, not adrenal blood.

questions.stem: During resection of an adrenal mass, the surgeon controls a vessel entering the gland midway along its medial border. This middle adrenal artery arises directly from which structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abdominal aorta

choices.label: B
choices.text: Renal artery

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inferior phrenic artery

choices.label: D
choices.text: Celiac trunk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Superior mesenteric artery

explanation.summary: The adrenal gland has three arterial sources: superior from the inferior phrenic, middle from the aorta, and inferior from the renal artery.
explanation.whyCorrect: The middle adrenal arteries branch directly off the abdominal aorta, which lies just medial to the left gland and near the midline behind the right. This direct aortic branch is one of three separate inflows that give the gland its rich arterial supply. Recognizing all three is important because each must be controlled during adrenalectomy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The renal arteries give rise to the inferior adrenal arteries, not the middle ones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The inferior phrenic arteries give rise to the superior adrenal arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The celiac trunk supplies foregut structures, including much of the pancreas through the splenic and common hepatic arteries.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The superior mesenteric artery supplies midgut structures and gives the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman has episodic headache, palpitations, tremor, and drenching sweats. Imaging shows a tumor arising from the central core of the right suprarenal gland. The cells of origin are best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Steroid-producing cortical cells that secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Steroid-producing cortical cells that secrete glucocorticoids and androgens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Islet-derived neuroendocrine cells that secrete somatostatin and glucagon

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modified sympathetic neurons that secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Modified sympathetic neurons that secrete mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids

explanation.summary: The adrenal medulla forms the central core of the gland and is made of modified sympathetic neurons that release catecholamines.
explanation.whyCorrect: The adrenal gland is organized into an outer cortex and a central medulla that differ in embryologic origin, microscopic structure, and hormone output. The medulla behaves as part of the autonomic nervous system and secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine. A catecholamine surge from a medullary tumor explains her episodic headache, palpitations, tremor, and sweating.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cortical cells make steroids; they do not synthesize catecholamines.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Glucocorticoids and androgens come from the cortex, which forms the outer portion rather than the central core.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Islet cells belong to the endocrine pancreas and are not found in the adrenal gland.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids are steroid products of the cortex, not of medullary neuronal cells.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man is scheduled for resection of the tail of the pancreas for a localized lesion. He asks whether removing that part of the organ will eliminate his ability to make insulin. Which statement about the endocrine pancreas best informs the answer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Islets of Langerhans form a discrete lobe along the pancreatic neck

choices.label: B
choices.text: Islets of Langerhans line the pancreatic duct throughout the whole gland

choices.label: C
choices.text: Islets of Langerhans are scattered throughout the head, body, and tail

choices.label: D
choices.text: Islets of Langerhans are confined to the tail near the splenic hilum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Islets of Langerhans are confined to the head within the duodenal curve

explanation.summary: The endocrine pancreas is not a gross anatomic region; it consists of microscopic islets dispersed through the entire gland.
explanation.whyCorrect: Within the predominantly exocrine pancreas, clusters of endocrine cells called the islets of Langerhans are distributed across the head, body, and tail. Because they are microscopic and diffuse rather than segregated into one region, removing the tail leaves islet tissue in the remaining pancreas. These islets produce insulin, glucagon, somatostatin, and pancreatic polypeptide directly into the bloodstream.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The neck is a narrow segment of the gland and contains no separate endocrine lobe.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ductal system is the exocrine drainage route; islets are not arranged along it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Islets are present well beyond the tail, so a distal segment does not hold the entire endocrine pancreas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The head contains islets, but it is not their exclusive location.

questions.stem: Insulin released from the islets of Langerhans enters the venous blood leaving the pancreas. This hormone-rich blood travels first into which venous circulation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cavernous sinus by way of the hypophyseal venous plexus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Portal venous system by way of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inferior vena cava by way of a single pancreatic vein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Left renal vein by way of the greater pancreatic vein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Brachiocephalic veins by way of the inferior thyroid veins

explanation.summary: Pancreatic venous blood, including islet hormone output, drains into the portal venous system through the splenic and superior mesenteric veins.
explanation.whyCorrect: Venous drainage of the pancreas parallels its arterial supply and empties into the splenic and superior mesenteric veins, which unite to form the portal vein. Islet hormones such as insulin therefore enter the portal circulation rather than draining directly into the systemic veins. This contrasts with the adrenal gland, whose single adrenal vein delivers blood straight into the systemic circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The cavernous sinus receives venous blood carrying pituitary hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pancreas has no single vein emptying into the inferior vena cava; its drainage is portal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The left renal vein receives the left adrenal vein, not pancreatic venous blood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The brachiocephalic veins receive the inferior thyroid veins from the neck.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy is brought for a well-child visit. He is healthy and active. On examination, there is a firm, painless, 3-cm midline neck mass just above the level of the hyoid bone that moves upward when he swallows or protrudes his tongue. Which of the following best explains the origin of this mass?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Failure of the ultimobranchial body to join the thyroid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Incomplete obliteration of a pharyngeal cleft laterally

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistence of a segment of the thyroglossal duct

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fragmentation of a parathyroid gland during its descent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Enlargement of a remnant of Rathke pouch in the neck

explanation.summary: A midline neck mass that elevates with swallowing or tongue protrusion is a thyroglossal duct cyst.
explanation.whyCorrect: The thyroid descends from the floor of the primitive pharynx while tethered to the tongue by the thyroglossal duct, which normally degenerates and leaves the foramen cecum. When a segment of that duct persists, it can form a cyst anywhere from the foramen cecum to the suprasternal notch, most often near the hyoid bone. Because the remnant retains its attachment along the tongue-to-neck tract, the mass moves superiorly with swallowing and tongue protrusion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ultimobranchial body supplies parafollicular C cells to the thyroid; its failure would affect calcitonin-producing cells, not create a mobile midline cyst.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pharyngeal cleft remnants produce lateral neck lesions, not a midline mass tethered to the tongue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Fragmented parathyroid tissue yields accessory or ectopic glands, typically clinically silent or mediastinal rather than a midline neck mass.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rathke pouch remnants remain intracranial in the sellar or parasellar region and do not descend into the neck.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl has a painless midline neck mass consistent with a thyroglossal duct cyst, and surgical excision is planned because of recurrent infections. Which of the following is the most important step before the cyst is removed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Confirm that the parathyroid glands are in normal position

choices.label: B
choices.text: Document that serum calcitonin concentration is normal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Document that the pyramidal lobe of the thyroid is absent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Confirm that normally located thyroid tissue is present

choices.label: E
choices.text: Establish that the mass moves with tongue protrusion

explanation.summary: A thyroglossal duct cyst may contain the patient's only functioning thyroid tissue, so normal thyroid must be confirmed before excision.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thyroid tissue can be found anywhere along the path of descent, and a thyroglossal duct remnant may harbor ectopic thyroid. If that ectopic tissue is the patient's only functioning thyroid, removing the cyst produces hypothyroidism. Imaging to confirm a normally positioned gland therefore precedes excision.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The parathyroids arise from pharyngeal pouch endoderm and are not part of the thyroglossal tract, so their position does not affect this operation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcitonin reflects parafollicular C-cell function and does not indicate whether normal thyroid tissue exists in the neck.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The pyramidal lobe is a common normal variant derived from the distal duct and is not a contraindication to excision.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Movement with tongue protrusion supports the diagnosis but does not address the risk of removing functioning thyroid tissue.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has months of worsening headache and nausea and is found on examination to have loss of vision in both temporal fields. MRI shows a suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. This tumor most likely arose from remnants of a structure derived from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neuroectoderm of the diencephalon

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oral ectoderm of the primitive mouth roof

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endoderm of the primitive pharyngeal floor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neural crest cells migrating from the neural tube

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mesoderm adjacent to the developing gonadal ridge

explanation.summary: Craniopharyngiomas arise from Rathke pouch remnants, which are oral ectoderm.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rathke pouch is an ectodermal outpouching from the roof of the primitive oral cavity that grows upward to become the anterior pituitary. Remnants left behind in the sella turcica or parasellar region can give rise to craniopharyngiomas, which are benign and slow growing. Their location explains the headache and nausea from raised intracranial pressure and the visual field loss from optic chiasm compression.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diencephalic neuroectoderm forms the posterior pituitary, which is neural tissue and not the source of these remnant-derived tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pharyngeal floor endoderm gives rise to the thyroid primordium, which descends into the neck rather than into the sella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Neural crest contributes the adrenal medulla and other chromaffin tissue, not the pituitary region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Mesoderm near the gonadal ridge contributes to gonadal and adrenal cortical tissue, not to sellar tumors.

questions.stem: An investigator studies a mouse embryo in which the downward extension of neural tissue from the developing brain fails to form, although the outpouching from the oral cavity roof develops normally. Deficiency of which of the following hormones is most likely in the mature animal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenocorticotropic hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolactin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antidiuretic hormone

explanation.summary: The posterior pituitary forms from a downgrowth of diencephalic neuroectoderm and releases ADH and oxytocin.
explanation.whyCorrect: As Rathke pouch grows upward, neural tissue extends downward from the diencephalon and carries hypothalamic axons that become the posterior lobe. Loss of that downgrowth eliminates the neurohypophysis, so ADH, which promotes renal water reabsorption, and oxytocin cannot be released. The oral outpouching is intact in this embryo, so the anterior lobe still forms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACTH is an anterior lobe product derived from the intact Rathke pouch tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Growth hormone is made by the anterior lobe, which develops normally in this embryo.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Prolactin is an anterior lobe hormone acting directly on target tissue and is unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TSH comes from anterior pituitary thyrotrophs and would still be produced.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old infant has a seizure. Serum calcium is low and serum phosphate is elevated; parathyroid hormone concentration is inappropriately low. He has had two episodes of pneumonia since birth, and imaging shows no thymic tissue. Abnormal development of which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Third and fourth pharyngeal pouches

choices.label: B
choices.text: First and second pharyngeal clefts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Midline floor of the primitive pharynx

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ultimobranchial body and its C cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neural crest cells populating the adrenal gland

explanation.summary: DiGeorge syndrome reflects failed development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, producing absent parathyroids and thymus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The parathyroid glands arise from endoderm of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, and the thymus develops in the same region. In 22q11 deletion syndrome these pouches develop abnormally, so the parathyroids are absent or hypoplastic and the thymus is aplastic. The result is hypocalcemia from hypoparathyroidism together with T-cell deficiency and recurrent infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Pharyngeal clefts are ectoderm-covered external grooves and do not give rise to parathyroid or thymic tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The midline pharyngeal floor produces the thyroid primordium; its failure causes thyroid agenesis, not hypocalcemia with absent thymus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ultimobranchial body supplies calcitonin-secreting C cells, whose loss would not cause hypocalcemia with low PTH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neural crest failure in the adrenal gland impairs catecholamine-producing chromaffin cells, not calcium regulation.

questions.stem: A 54-year-old woman with hypercalcemia and an elevated parathyroid hormone concentration undergoes neck exploration, but only three parathyroid glands are identified and the hypercalcemia persists. Imaging of which of the following locations is most likely to reveal the responsible gland?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Base of the tongue, near the foramen cecum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Along the carotid sheath above the hyoid bone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anterior mediastinum, near thymic tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Within the isthmus of the thyroid gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: Posterior mediastinum, adjacent to the esophagus

explanation.summary: Inferior parathyroid glands descend with the thymus, so ectopic glands are classically found in the anterior mediastinum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The inferior parathyroids arise from the third pharyngeal pouch and travel with the thymus into the lower neck, a longer migration than the superior glands make. Abnormal migration can therefore carry an inferior gland into the anterior mediastinum alongside thymic tissue. This is the classic ectopic site that complicates localization in hyperparathyroidism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The tongue base is the classic site of ectopic thyroid tissue, not of parathyroid glands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The parathyroid migration path follows the thymus inferiorly rather than tracking upward along the carotid sheath.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parathyroid glands lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid; the isthmus is the expected site of a pyramidal lobe instead.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The descent that carries an inferior gland out of the neck follows the thymus into the anterior, not posterior, mediastinum.

questions.stem: During a neck dissection, a parathyroid gland is identified at the upper pole of the posterior thyroid surface. This gland is derived from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Third pharyngeal pouch endoderm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Second pharyngeal pouch endoderm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neural crest mesenchyme of the arches

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fourth pharyngeal pouch endoderm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mesoderm of the pharyngeal arches

explanation.summary: The superior parathyroid glands come from the fourth pharyngeal pouch; the inferior glands come from the third.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both parathyroid pairs develop from pharyngeal pouch endoderm and settle on the posterior surface of the thyroid. The fourth pouch supplies the superior glands, which migrate only a short distance. The third pouch supplies the inferior glands, which descend farther with the thymus, which is why glands that originate higher end up lower in the adult.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Third pouch endoderm gives rise to the inferior parathyroid glands, which end up at the lower pole.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The second pouch does not contribute parathyroid tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neural crest mesenchyme contributes to arch structures and the adrenal medulla, not to parathyroid epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Arch mesoderm forms muscle and connective tissue rather than pouch-derived endocrine glands.

questions.stem: A newborn girl has ambiguous genitalia, and by the second week of life she develops vomiting, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. Serum cortisol is low and ACTH is markedly elevated, and the adrenal glands are enlarged bilaterally. The hyperplastic tissue in this infant is derived from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neural crest

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mesoderm

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endoderm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surface ectoderm

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neuroectoderm

explanation.summary: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia expands the adrenal cortex, which is mesodermal in origin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enzyme deficiencies that impair cortisol synthesis remove negative feedback, so ACTH rises and drives hyperplasia of the adrenal cortex. Severe forms present in infancy with salt loss and abnormal genital development, as in this infant. The cortex, which makes cortisol, aldosterone, and androgen precursors, derives from mesoderm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neural crest gives rise to the adrenal medulla and its chromaffin cells, which are not the tissue driven by ACTH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endoderm forms the thyroid, parathyroids, and pancreas, not adrenal tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surface ectoderm contributes structures such as Rathke pouch in the head, not the adrenal gland.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuroectoderm of the diencephalon forms the posterior pituitary rather than any part of the adrenal.

questions.stem: An investigator studying human fetal development examines the adrenal gland at 9 weeks of gestation and finds a large inner zone surrounded by a thinner outer cortical layer. Which of the following best describes the function of the large inner zone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It produces catecholamines that support fetal cardiovascular tone

choices.label: B
choices.text: It produces aldosterone that maintains fetal sodium balance

choices.label: C
choices.text: It produces cortisol that drives late fetal organ maturation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces calcitonin that regulates fetal skeletal mineralization

choices.label: E
choices.text: It produces androgen precursors for placental estrogen synthesis

explanation.summary: The fetal zone of the adrenal cortex makes androgen precursors for placental estrogen production and then regresses.
explanation.whyCorrect: By weeks 8 to 9 a large fetal zone forms inside a thinner outer cortical layer. The fetal zone supplies androgen precursors that support placental estrogen production and fetal reproductive development. Late in gestation it regresses, while the outer layer becomes the permanent cortex and its rising cortisol output contributes to organ maturation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Catecholamines come from neural crest-derived chromaffin cells of the medulla, a separate compartment from the fetal zone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aldosterone production belongs to the zona glomerulosa, which differentiates from the outer cortex around birth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rising cortisol late in gestation comes from the outer cortical layer as the fetal zone is regressing.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Calcitonin is a thyroid C-cell product and is not made by any part of the adrenal gland.

questions.stem: A healthy 2-day-old newborn undergoes autopsy after an unrelated accidental death, and the adrenal cortex is examined histologically. Which of the following findings is most consistent with normal adrenal development at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All three cortical zones fully developed in their adult arrangement

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zona reticularis present, with the outer two zones not yet differentiated

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glomerulosa and fasciculata present, reticularis not yet formed

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cortex still separate from the medulla, which lies outside the capsule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fetal zone still occupying most of the cortical volume

explanation.summary: At birth the outer cortex has differentiated into zona glomerulosa and fasciculata; the zona reticularis appears after birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: The adrenal gland is not fully mature at birth and continues developing through early childhood. At birth the outer cortex differentiates into the zona glomerulosa and zona fasciculata, and the zona reticularis develops afterward. Adult zonal organization is reached at roughly 3 years of age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adult zonation is not achieved until about 3 years of age, not at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The zona reticularis is the last zone to appear, developing after the outer two zones are established.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The expanding cortex surrounds and encapsulates the medulla during development, so by birth the medulla is internal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The fetal zone regresses rapidly late in fetal life and does not dominate the cortex after delivery.

questions.stem: A newborn boy has bilious vomiting on the first day of life. Imaging shows a ring of pancreatic tissue completely encircling the second part of the duodenum with proximal obstruction. Which of the following developmental events best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abnormal rotation of the ventral pancreatic bud around the duodenum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Failure of the dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds to fuse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Failure of the endocrine pancreas to separate from the exocrine tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistence of a duct connecting the pancreas to the foregut

choices.label: E
choices.text: Migration of neural crest cells into the developing pancreatic buds

explanation.summary: Annular pancreas results from abnormal rotation of the ventral bud, which encircles the duodenum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pancreas forms from dorsal and ventral buds of distal foregut endoderm, and during gut rotation the ventral bud normally swings posteriorly around the duodenum to fuse with the dorsal bud. When that rotation is abnormal, pancreatic tissue surrounds the duodenum as a ring. The encircling tissue can constrict the duodenum and cause obstruction.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Failure of the two buds to fuse produces pancreas divisum, in which drainage occurs through separate ducts without an encircling ring.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endocrine and exocrine cells both differentiate from bud endoderm and are normally intermingled, so no separation step is missing here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The duct remnant that persists along a migration path is a thyroid phenomenon, not a cause of duodenal encirclement.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neural crest cells populate the adrenal medulla; they are not the source of the pancreatic tissue forming this ring.

questions.stem: A researcher isolates islets of Langerhans from a human fetal pancreas and confirms that the cells secrete insulin and glucagon. These cells are derived from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endoderm of the fourth pharyngeal pouch

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mesoderm surrounding the developing gut

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neural crest cells that migrate into the gut

choices.label: D
choices.text: Endoderm of the distal foregut

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neuroectoderm of the developing diencephalon

explanation.summary: Both the endocrine and exocrine pancreas arise from endoderm of the distal foregut.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dorsal and ventral pancreatic buds arise from distal foregut endoderm, and endoderm from those buds differentiates into both endocrine and exocrine pancreatic cells. The islets of Langerhans, which secrete insulin and glucagon along with smaller amounts of somatostatin and amylin, are therefore endodermal.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fourth pouch endoderm gives rise to the superior parathyroids and the ultimobranchial body, not to pancreatic islets.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mesoderm gives rise to the adrenal cortex and supporting tissues rather than to islet cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neural crest supplies chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla, not insulin- or glucagon-secreting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Diencephalic neuroectoderm forms the posterior pituitary and has no role in pancreatic development.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has 8 months of amenorrhea and fatigue. MRI shows a 2-cm nonfunctioning suprasellar mass compressing the pituitary stalk. Laboratory studies show a low free T4, a low morning cortisol, and a low serum IGF-1. Which of the following serum hormones is most likely to be elevated in this patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adrenocorticotropic hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Follicle-stimulating hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prolactin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thyroid-stimulating hormone

explanation.summary: Prolactin is under tonic dopaminergic inhibition, so interrupting hypothalamic input raises prolactin while every stimulated pituitary hormone falls.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dopamine travels from the hypothalamus down the stalk to tonically suppress prolactin release. A mass that compresses the stalk removes that inhibition, so prolactin rises. Every other anterior pituitary hormone depends on a stimulatory releasing hormone arriving through the same portal route, so they fall instead, which is exactly the low free T4, low cortisol, and low IGF-1 pattern described.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACTH depends on CRH arriving through the portal vessels, so stalk compression lowers it, as reflected in this patient's low cortisol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FSH depends on hypothalamic GnRH, so loss of stalk delivery lowers it and explains the amenorrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GH depends on GHRH stimulation, and the low IGF-1 already indicates that GH output has fallen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TSH depends on TRH reaching the thyrotrophs, so it falls and leaves this patient with a low free T4.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old woman has several months of fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance. Laboratory studies show a serum TSH of 22 microunits/mL (elevated) and a low free T4. Which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypothalamic TRH-secreting neurons

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anterior pituitary thyrotrophs

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypophyseal portal vessels

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thyroid gland

choices.label: E
choices.text: Posterior pituitary axon terminals

explanation.summary: A low target hormone paired with a high tropic hormone is primary failure: the target gland has failed while the pituitary compensates.
explanation.whyCorrect: The failure-level map uses the tropic hormone, not the target hormone, as the diagnostic key. Because the thyroid cannot make T3/T4, negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary is lost, and the intact pituitary drives TSH upward. High TSH with low free T4 therefore localizes the failure to the tier 3 target gland.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of TRH removes the drive to the thyrotrophs, so TSH would be inappropriately normal or low rather than markedly elevated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Failure of the thyrotrophs means TSH cannot rise, giving low free T4 with low TSH, which is secondary hypothyroidism.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interrupting portal delivery cuts off TRH, again producing an inappropriately low TSH rather than a high one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin and has no role in the thyroid axis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman is evaluated 6 weeks after a delivery complicated by severe postpartum hemorrhage. She was never able to breastfeed and now reports fatigue and lightheadedness. Laboratory studies show low free T4 with low TSH, low cortisol with low ACTH, and low LH and FSH. Urine output and serum sodium are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Postpartum infarction of the anterior pituitary

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of vasopressin release from the posterior pituitary

choices.label: E
choices.text: Autonomous cortisol secretion by an adrenal adenoma

explanation.summary: Sheehan syndrome infarcts the anterior pituitary, so every tropic hormone falls together with its target hormone while the posterior lobe is spared.
explanation.whyCorrect: Postpartum pituitary infarction knocks out the whole anterior lobe at once, producing global secondary failure: TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, and GH all drop alongside their target hormones. Failed lactation from loss of prolactin is often the first clue. The posterior pituitary has a separate blood supply and is typically spared, which is why her urine output and sodium are normal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Primary thyroid failure would raise TSH as the intact pituitary compensates, and it would not explain the low ACTH and low gonadotropins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary adrenal failure produces low cortisol with a high ACTH, the opposite of the pattern here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Loss of ADH causes polyuria with dilute urine and rising sodium, neither of which is present.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An autonomous cortisol-secreting adenoma raises cortisol and suppresses ACTH, whereas this patient's cortisol is low.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has heat intolerance, a 6-kg weight loss, and tremor. Laboratory studies show an elevated free T4 and an undetectable TSH. Thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins are present in high titer. Which of the following best explains the undetectable TSH?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pituitary has lost the ability to sense circulating thyroid hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Feedback is intact and suppressing TSH but cannot suppress the antibody

choices.label: C
choices.text: The antibodies bind pituitary thyrotrophs and block TSH synthesis directly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hypothalamic somatostatin has risen and shut down all thyrotroph output

choices.label: E
choices.text: The thyroid is releasing a protease that degrades TSH in the circulation

explanation.summary: In Graves disease the feedback loop works perfectly; it simply cannot suppress a stimulus that lies outside pituitary control.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thyroid-stimulating antibodies mimic TSH and drive the thyroid gland directly. The pituitary correctly detects the rising T3/T4 and suppresses TSH to undetectable levels, but the antibody keeps stimulating the gland regardless. Hormone levels therefore rise unchecked not because feedback failed, but because the driving signal is not something the pituitary can turn off.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pituitary blind to thyroid hormone would fail to suppress TSH; here TSH is suppressed exactly as expected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The stimulating immunoglobulins act on the thyroid TSH receptor, not on pituitary thyrotrophs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatostatin is hypothalamus-driven inhibitory tone independent of the target gland and is not what suppresses TSH in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The low TSH reflects reduced pituitary secretion from negative feedback, not destruction of circulating hormone.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has been taking high-dose prednisone for 6 weeks for a systemic vasculitis. Which of the following best describes the expected state of his hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated CRH with a normal ACTH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated ACTH with a low cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Suppressed CRH and suppressed ACTH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevated ACTH with a normal CRH

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unchanged CRH and unchanged ACTH

explanation.summary: Exogenous glucocorticoids mimic cortisol and trigger long-loop negative feedback at both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary.
explanation.whyCorrect: Target-gland hormones feed back to suppress both tiers above them. Prednisone behaves like circulating cortisol, so it binds receptors in the hypothalamus and pituitary and reduces CRH and ACTH secretion together. Chronic suppression of this kind is the mechanism behind tertiary adrenal insufficiency when steroids are withdrawn.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Elevated CRH ignores the fact that feedback from a glucocorticoid acts on the hypothalamus first.
whyWrongByChoice.B: High ACTH with low cortisol is the pattern of primary adrenal failure, not exogenous steroid use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Elevated ACTH would require loss of feedback, whereas this patient has an excess of glucocorticoid signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An unchanged axis would mean negative feedback is not operating, which is inconsistent with intact feedback receptors.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has central obesity, purple abdominal striae, and new hypertension. Laboratory studies show a markedly elevated 24-hour urinary free cortisol and an undetectable plasma ACTH. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A corticotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary

choices.label: B
choices.text: A hypothalamic tumor secreting excess CRH

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex

choices.label: D
choices.text: A small cell lung carcinoma secreting ACTH ectopically

choices.label: E
choices.text: An adrenal adenoma secreting cortisol autonomously

explanation.summary: High target hormone with a suppressed tropic hormone is primary overproduction, meaning the target gland is making hormone autonomously.
explanation.whyCorrect: An adrenal adenoma produces cortisol independently of any upstream signal. The intact pituitary senses the high cortisol and suppresses ACTH through negative feedback, giving high cortisol with undetectable ACTH. That combination is the fingerprint of Cushing syndrome from an adrenal source rather than a pituitary-driven process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A corticotroph adenoma drives the adrenal gland, so both ACTH and cortisol would be high (secondary overproduction).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Excess CRH would drive ACTH upward as well, which contradicts the undetectable ACTH.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adrenal destruction lowers cortisol and raises ACTH, the reverse of this patient's labs.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An ectopic ACTH source raises measured plasma ACTH along with cortisol.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man is hospitalized after a traumatic brain injury. Over the next 2 days he produces 6 L of dilute urine per day and drinks water constantly. Serum sodium is 149 mEq/L and urine osmolality is low. The hormone he is lacking normally reaches the circulation by which of the following routes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Secretion by posterior pituitary gland cells after tropic stimulation

choices.label: B
choices.text: Axonal transport from hypothalamic neurons to posterior pituitary terminals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hypophyseal portal vessels carrying it to the anterior pituitary

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release from anterior pituitary cells into the systemic circulation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Diffusion from hypothalamic capillaries straight into systemic blood

explanation.summary: ADH is made in hypothalamic neurons and released from their axon terminals in the posterior pituitary, with no gland or tropic hormone in between.
explanation.whyCorrect: This patient has central diabetes insipidus from loss of ADH release. The posterior pituitary is neural tissue: supraoptic and paraventricular neurons synthesize ADH, transport it down their axons through the infundibulum, and store it in dense-core vesicles seen as Herring bodies until action potentials trigger release. The hypothalamic neuron is the gland, so there is no tropic hormone to measure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The posterior pituitary does not synthesize or secrete hormone on its own; it is a release site for hypothalamic products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Portal vessels serve only the anterior pituitary and carry hypothalamic releasing hormones, not ADH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The anterior pituitary releases FSH, LH, ACTH, TSH, prolactin, and GH, none of which is ADH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hypothalamic hormones do not spill directly into systemic circulation; ADH follows the axonal route to its terminals.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is in the final stage of labor. Cervical stretch triggers oxytocin release, the resulting uterine contractions increase cervical stretch further, and oxytocin release intensifies. Which of the following best characterizes this control mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Long-loop negative feedback from a target-gland hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Short-loop negative feedback acting on the hypothalamus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tonic dopaminergic inhibition lifted by neural input

choices.label: D
choices.text: Positive feedback, in which the output reinforces the stimulus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tropic amplification across three sequential endocrine tiers

explanation.summary: Both major oxytocin actions, uterine contraction in labor and the milk-ejection reflex, are governed by positive feedback.
explanation.whyCorrect: In labor, cervical stretch drives oxytocin release, oxytocin drives contraction, and contraction produces more cervical stretch, so the output amplifies rather than opposes the original stimulus. The lactation counterpart works the same way: continued suckling sustains reflex oxytocin pulses that eject milk. This is the opposite of the negative feedback that governs the anterior pituitary axes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Long-loop negative feedback describes a target-gland hormone suppressing the hypothalamus and pituitary, which would terminate rather than intensify the response.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Short-loop feedback is a pituitary tropic hormone suppressing hypothalamic releasing-hormone output, and oxytocin release here is escalating.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dopaminergic inhibition applies to prolactin in the anterior pituitary, not to oxytocin release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxytocin has no releasing hormone, no tropic hormone, and no target-gland tier to amplify through.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man is admitted with dehydration. Plasma osmolality is 305 mOsm/kg and plasma vasopressin is elevated. After several hours of water intake, plasma osmolality falls to 285 mOsm/kg and plasma vasopressin returns to normal. Which of the following best explains why vasopressin secretion fell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Falling plasma osmolality sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Long-loop feedback from a hormone secreted by the kidney

choices.label: C
choices.text: Short-loop feedback of vasopressin on anterior pituitary cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dopaminergic inhibition of the posterior pituitary axon terminals

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppression of the pituitary tropic hormone that drives vasopressin

explanation.summary: For vasopressin, the negative feedback signal is the physiological variable itself, not a downstream hormone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Osmoreceptors sense rising plasma osmolality and baroreceptors sense falling volume; either drives ADH release. ADH promotes renal water reabsorption, which lowers osmolality and restores volume, and that correction removes the very stimulus that started the process. Once osmolality returns toward the set point, the afferent signal disappears and ADH secretion falls.

whyWrongByChoice.B: No renal hormone feeds back on ADH; the regulated variable itself closes the loop.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Short-loop feedback belongs to the anterior pituitary axes, and vasopressin does not act on anterior pituitary cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dopamine inhibits prolactin in the anterior pituitary and does not regulate posterior pituitary release.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no tropic hormone in the posterior pituitary pathway; the hypothalamic neuron releases ADH directly.

questions.stem: Which of the following hypothalamic signals suppresses release of both growth hormone and thyroid-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary, independently of what the target glands are doing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dopamine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin-like growth factor-1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Somatostatin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Triiodothyronine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Corticotropin-releasing hormone

explanation.summary: Somatostatin is hypothalamic inhibitory tone, a parallel mechanism distinct from negative feedback, and it suppresses GH and TSH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Dopamine and somatostatin are released by the hypothalamus to suppress pituitary output; the signal originates at the top and travels down, regardless of target-gland activity. Somatostatin is the one that suppresses both GH and TSH release. This is not feedback, because feedback originates from a target hormone traveling backward up the axis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Dopamine is hypothalamic inhibitory tone as well, but its target is prolactin rather than GH and TSH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IGF-1 is a liver-derived feedback signal traveling up the axis, and it does not suppress TSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Triiodothyronine is a target-gland hormone providing long-loop feedback on TRH and TSH, not a hypothalamic inhibitory signal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CRH is a stimulatory releasing hormone that drives ACTH secretion.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old woman is being evaluated for suspected hypothalamic-pituitary disease. Serum TSH and free T4 are obtained, but serum thyrotropin-releasing hormone is not measured. Which of the following best explains why TRH is not measured in the blood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is stored in Herring bodies and released only in brief bursts

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reaches the pituitary through direct neuronal synapses rather than blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is degraded by the anterior pituitary before entering any vessel

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its concentration in blood always mirrors the measured TSH concentration

choices.label: E
choices.text: It travels in hypophyseal portal blood, which cannot be sampled

explanation.summary: Hypothalamic releasing hormones act through a short portal circulation that is inaccessible to sampling, so clinicians use tropic and target hormones instead.
explanation.whyCorrect: TRH travels only the short distance from the hypothalamus to the anterior pituitary through the hypophyseal portal vessels, a specialized portal blood system. Because portal blood cannot be sampled clinically, releasing hormones are not routinely measured. Localization is done instead by pairing the pituitary tropic hormone with the target-gland hormone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herring bodies are storage sites for oxytocin and ADH at posterior pituitary axon terminals, not for TRH.
whyWrongByChoice.B: TRH is a hormone carried in portal blood; the pituitary is reached through vessels, not synapses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The barrier to measurement is the inaccessibility of portal blood, not degradation within the pituitary.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TRH and TSH move in opposite directions in pituitary disease, which is why the pair is informative at all.

questions.stem: A healthy 19-year-old man has a growth hormone pulse that stimulates hepatocytes to secrete insulin-like growth factor-1. Which of the following effects does the resulting rise in circulating IGF-1 have on the somatotropic axis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Increases GHRH from the hypothalamus and GH from the pituitary

choices.label: B
