choices.text: Suppresses GHRH from the hypothalamus and GH from the pituitary

choices.label: C
choices.text: Suppresses GH from the pituitary but leaves GHRH secretion unchanged

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increases hepatic GH receptor density without altering GHRH secretion

choices.label: E
choices.text: Suppresses GHRH only after being converted back into growth hormone

explanation.summary: IGF-1 is the target hormone of the GH axis and exerts long-loop negative feedback on both the hypothalamus and the anterior pituitary.
explanation.whyCorrect: GH stimulates hepatocytes to secrete IGF-1, and both GH and IGF-1 feed back to the hypothalamus to suppress GHRH and to the anterior pituitary to suppress GH. This is the same long-loop pattern seen with T3/T4 on TRH and TSH and with cortisol on CRH and ACTH. Suppressing both tiers is what keeps GH output near its set point.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rising target hormone reduces, rather than increases, releasing and tropic hormone output.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Long-loop feedback suppresses the hypothalamus as well, so GHRH does not stay unchanged.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lecture describes feedback suppression of GHRH and GH, not upregulation of hepatic GH receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IGF-1 is not converted into GH; it acts as a feedback signal in its own right.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man is evaluated for enlarging hands and feet, coarsening facial features, and a widening gap between his teeth. MRI shows a 9-mm sellar mass, and resection reveals a benign pituitary adenoma. On hematoxylin and eosin staining, the tumor is composed of sheets of pink-staining cells. Proliferation of which of the following cell types best explains this patient's presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acidophils

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chromophobes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pituicytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Chief cells

explanation.summary: Acidophils of the anterior pituitary stain pink with eosin and produce growth hormone and prolactin.
explanation.whyCorrect: The anterior lobe contains three cell types named for how they stain, and acidophils take up eosin and appear pink. Acidophils secrete growth hormone and prolactin, and a functional adenoma made of them raises the corresponding hormone level. Growth hormone excess produces gigantism in children and acromegaly in adults, which matches this man's enlarging hands, feet, and facial bones.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Basophils stain bluish-purple with hematoxylin and make FSH, LH, ACTH, and TSH, none of which cause acral overgrowth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chromophobes stain poorly with either dye and produce no hormone, so they cannot drive a hormone excess syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pituicytes are support cells of the posterior lobe that maintain axons rather than secrete hormones.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chief cells belong to the parathyroid gland and secrete parathyroid hormone, not growth hormone.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman undergoes transsphenoidal resection of a pituitary adenoma. Histologic sections show glandular cells that stain deeply bluish-purple with hematoxylin. Excess of which of the following hormones is most consistent with the staining pattern of this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Growth hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prolactin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Corticotropin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antidiuretic hormone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oxytocin

explanation.summary: Basophils stain with hematoxylin and secrete the B-FLAT hormones: FSH, LH, ACTH, and TSH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anterior pituitary cells are classified by their staining, and the hematoxylin-avid basophils appear bluish-purple. Their products are remembered as B-FLAT: Basophils make FSH, LH, ACTH, and TSH. ACTH is therefore the only listed hormone that a basophilic adenoma would overproduce.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth hormone comes from acidophils, which stain pink with eosin rather than purple with hematoxylin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Prolactin is the other acidophil product and would be expected in a pink, eosin-staining tumor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ADH is made by hypothalamic secretory neurons and only stored in the posterior lobe, not made by anterior lobe glandular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxytocin is likewise produced in the hypothalamus and stored in the neurohypophysis, so no adenohypophyseal cell secretes it.

questions.stem: A pituitary specimen from a 61-year-old man contains clusters of anterior lobe cells that take up neither hematoxylin nor eosin well and therefore appear pale. Which of the following best describes these pale cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mixed group of stem, progenitor, and degranulated cells that secrete no hormone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eosin-avid glandular cells that secrete growth hormone and prolactin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hematoxylin-avid glandular cells that secrete FSH, LH, ACTH, and TSH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Modified sympathetic neurons that secrete epinephrine into capillaries

choices.label: E
choices.text: Support cells whose nuclei lie scattered among unmyelinated axons

explanation.summary: Chromophobes are the pale, poorly staining anterior pituitary cells and produce no hormone.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chromophobes are defined by their failure to stain well with either hematoxylin or eosin, giving them a pale appearance. They are a heterogeneous population that includes stem cells, undifferentiated progenitor cells, and degranulated cells. They do not produce any hormone, which distinguishes them from the other two anterior lobe cell types.

whyWrongByChoice.B: That describes acidophils, which stain pink with eosin rather than appearing pale.
whyWrongByChoice.C: That describes basophils, which stain bluish-purple with hematoxylin rather than appearing pale.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromaffin cells with those features are found in the adrenal medulla, not in the pituitary.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pituicytes support axons in the posterior lobe, whereas these cells are in the glandular anterior lobe.

questions.stem: A section through the pars nervosa of the pituitary shows long, thin, string-like processes interspersed with large, rounded, pink structures. The hormones stored within those pink structures are synthesized in which of the following locations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acidophils of the anterior lobe

choices.label: B
choices.text: Basophils of the anterior lobe

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pituicytes within the posterior lobe

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parafollicular cells of the thyroid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory neurons of the hypothalamus

explanation.summary: Herring bodies are dilated axon terminals in the posterior pituitary that store oxytocin and ADH made in the hypothalamus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The posterior lobe is not glandular; it is roughly 100,000 nerve axons, and the large pink Herring bodies are their dilated terminal portions. Oxytocin and ADH are produced by secretory neurons whose cell bodies sit in the hypothalamus. The hormones travel down those axons to the neurohypophysis, where they are stored in Herring bodies until release.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acidophils make growth hormone and prolactin, which are released from the anterior lobe and never stored in Herring bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Basophils make the B-FLAT hormones in the anterior lobe, a separate glandular compartment.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pituicytes are glial-type support cells for the axons; they keep the axons healthy but do not synthesize hormone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parafollicular cells secrete calcitonin in the thyroid gland, unrelated to the neurohypophysis.

questions.stem: A thyroid biopsy from a 34-year-old woman shows abundant round follicles, each lined by simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium and filled centrally with a pink, gelatinous material. Which of the following is the primary function of that central material?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Synthesizing thyroid hormone from circulating precursors

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secreting calcitonin in response to a rising serum calcium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Storing thyroid hormone until the body requires it

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supporting the epithelial cells and keeping them healthy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Storing oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone before their release

explanation.summary: Colloid is the gelatinous follicular content that serves as the thyroid's hormone storage depot.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each thyroid follicle is lined by simple cuboidal to columnar epithelium and holds pink, gelatinous colloid. Thyroid hormone made by the follicular epithelial cells is stored in large quantities in that colloid. When hormone is needed, the epithelial cells ingest colloid, extract the hormone, and secrete it into the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Synthesis is carried out by the follicular epithelial cells lining the follicle, not by the colloid they surround.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Calcitonin comes from scattered parafollicular C cells located next to follicles, not from colloid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A supportive maintenance role describes pituicytes in the posterior pituitary, not thyroid colloid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oxytocin and ADH are stored in Herring bodies of the posterior pituitary, a different organ entirely.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a thyroid nodule, and laboratory studies show a markedly elevated serum calcitonin with a low-normal serum calcium. Thyroid hormone levels are normal. This tumor most likely arose from which of the following cell types?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Follicular epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parafollicular C cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parathyroid chief cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parathyroid oxyphil cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adrenal chromaffin cells

explanation.summary: Calcitonin comes from the thyroid's parafollicular (C) cells and acts to decrease serum calcium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Scattered among the thyroid follicles are parafollicular cells, called C cells because they secrete calcitonin; they sit alongside follicles and can be hard to identify on routine sections. Calcitonin has nothing to do with thyroid hormone, which is why the thyroid function tests are normal here. It is a regulatory hormone that decreases serum calcium, explaining the low-normal calcium in the setting of calcitonin excess.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Follicular epithelial cells synthesize thyroid hormone and store it in colloid; a tumor of these cells would not raise calcitonin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone, which raises rather than lowers serum calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oxyphil cells are parathyroid cells that make only low levels of PTH, not calcitonin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla secrete epinephrine and norepinephrine, not calcium-regulating hormones.

questions.stem: A 49-year-old woman has persistent hypocalcemia requiring intravenous calcium one day after total thyroidectomy for thyroid cancer. Review of the resected specimen shows normal colloid-filled follicles and, at one edge, sheets of compact cells with minimal cytoplasm together with clusters of large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm. Which of the following best explains her low serum calcium?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inadvertent removal of the parathyroid glands with loss of PTH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ongoing calcitonin release from residual parafollicular C cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of thyroid follicular epithelium and its stored colloid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Surgical injury to the adrenal cortex with mineralocorticoid deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Interruption of ADH release from the posterior pituitary

explanation.summary: Compact chief cells and eosinophilic oxyphil cells in a thyroidectomy specimen mean parathyroid tissue was removed, causing hypocalcemia.
explanation.whyCorrect: The parathyroid glands sit on the posterior surface of the thyroid, so they can be taken inadvertently during thyroidectomy. Chief cells are compact cells with minimal cytoplasm arranged in sheets, and oxyphil cells are large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm in clusters, so both described populations are parathyroid, not thyroid. Chief cells secrete parathyroid hormone, which increases calcium absorption and raises serum calcium; losing them drops the calcium level.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The C cells that secrete calcium-lowering calcitonin were removed with the thyroid, so residual C-cell activity is not the explanation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of follicular epithelium and colloid causes thyroid hormone deficiency, which does not lower serum calcium.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The adrenal glands sit atop the kidneys and are nowhere near the operative field of a thyroidectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: ADH from the neurohypophysis regulates water balance and is not disturbed by neck surgery.

questions.stem: A parathyroid gland removed from a 74-year-old man contains scattered clusters of large cells with abundant, brightly eosinophilic cytoplasm; such clusters were far less prominent in a gland examined from a young adult. Which of the following best characterizes these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Degenerated derivatives of chief cells that still make low levels of PTH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Principal secretory cells that carry out the gland's hormone production

choices.label: C
choices.text: Adipose cells that progressively replace the gland's secretory tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: Follicular cells that store their hormone product in surrounding colloid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Modified sympathetic neurons that release catecholamines into capillaries

explanation.summary: Oxyphil cells are large, eosinophilic parathyroid cells that accumulate with age and are degenerated chief cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The parathyroid contains chief cells, oxyphil cells, and interspersed adipose cells. Oxyphil cells are large cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm that occur in clusters and accumulate with age, matching both the appearance and the age difference described. They are degenerated derivatives of chief cells, with some still exhibiting low levels of PTH synthesis.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The functional workhorses of the gland are the chief cells, which are compact with minimal cytoplasm rather than large and eosinophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Adipose cells are present in the parathyroid but appear as clear fat cells, not as eosinophilic clusters.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Colloid-storing follicular cells belong to the thyroid gland, not the parathyroid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Catecholamine-secreting chromaffin cells are found in the adrenal medulla.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old man develops hyperglycemia after selective autoimmune destruction of the most numerous cell type within the islets of Langerhans, which normally makes up 70% to 75% of islet cells. Deficiency of which of the following hormones best accounts for his presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Glucagon and somatostatin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin and amylin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Somatostatin and ghrelin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ghrelin and pancreatic polypeptide

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pancreatic polypeptide and glucagon

explanation.summary: Beta cells are the most numerous islet cell type and secrete insulin and amylin.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each islet of Langerhans contains five cell types, of which beta cells are the most numerous at 70% to 75% of the total. Beta cells make insulin and amylin, and insulin is central to regulating serum glucose levels and glucose storage. Losing this population therefore produces hyperglycemia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Glucagon comes from alpha cells and somatostatin from delta cells, neither of which is the predominant islet population.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Somatostatin is a delta cell product and ghrelin an epsilon cell product; these are minority populations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ghrelin comes from epsilon cells and pancreatic polypeptide from PP cells, both minor islet constituents.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PP cells and alpha cells together still do not represent the dominant islet cell type.

questions.stem: A pancreatic islet cell tumor in a 57-year-old woman is found to secrete large amounts of ghrelin. Electron microscopy is required to confirm the cell of origin, because on light microscopy the islet cells all appear as small, rounded cells in clusters. This tumor most likely arose from which of the following islet cell types?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alpha cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beta cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delta cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epsilon cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: PP cells

explanation.summary: Epsilon cells are the ghrelin-producing cells of the islets of Langerhans.
explanation.whyCorrect: The five islet cell types each have a defined secretory product, and epsilon cells make ghrelin. Because the five types are indistinguishable on light microscopy, where they all appear as small, rounded cells in clusters, electron microscopy is needed to tell them apart. The hormone secreted therefore identifies the cell of origin.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha cells make glucagon, one of the two classic regulators of serum glucose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta cells, the most numerous islet cells, make insulin and amylin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delta cells make somatostatin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PP cells, also called gamma or F cells, make pancreatic polypeptide.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has not had a growth spurt or her first menstrual period. Imaging shows a small adrenal mass, and workup demonstrates deficient production of dehydroepiandrosterone. The lesion most likely involves which of the following regions of the adrenal gland?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zona glomerulosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zona fasciculata

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zona reticularis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adrenal medulla

choices.label: E
choices.text: Adrenal capsule

explanation.summary: The zona reticularis is the innermost cortical layer and secretes sex steroids such as DHEA.
explanation.whyCorrect: The adrenal cortex is layered from outside in as glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis (GFR). The zona reticularis is composed of compact cells arranged in a meandering, net-like pattern, and it secretes sex steroids such as DHEA. Those hormones are involved in development and function of the reproductive system, so their loss explains absent puberty.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The zona glomerulosa secretes mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone, which regulate blood pressure and sodium and potassium levels.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The zona fasciculata secretes glucocorticoids such as cortisol, which regulate blood pressure, metabolism, and immune function during stress.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The medulla secretes epinephrine and norepinephrine for the fight-or-flight response, not sex steroids.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsule is the connective tissue covering of the gland and secretes no hormone.

questions.stem: A section through an adrenal gland is examined. The innermost region contains clusters of cells that are modified sympathetic neurons and therefore lack axons and dendrites; they discharge their secretory product directly into adjacent capillaries. Which of the following do these cells secrete?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aldosterone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cortisol

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dehydroepiandrosterone

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epinephrine

choices.label: E
choices.text: Calcitonin

explanation.summary: The adrenal medulla is made of chromaffin cells, modified sympathetic neurons that release epinephrine and norepinephrine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The medulla lies deep to the cortex and is composed of clusters of chromaffin cells, which are modified sympathetic neurons and consequently lack axons and dendrites. On detecting a threat, they secrete a burst of adrenaline directly into capillaries. The result is an increase in heart rate, blood pressure, and blood sugar with blood flow redirected to muscle.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid from the zona glomerulosa, the thin outermost cortical layer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cortisol is a glucocorticoid from the zona fasciculata, the thick middle cortical layer of lipid-laden cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: DHEA is a sex steroid from the zona reticularis, the innermost layer of the cortex.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Calcitonin is secreted by parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland, not by any adrenal cell.

questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl is seen for a routine physical examination. Her breasts show enlargement in which the areola forms a secondary mound above the contour of the breast. Her pubic hair is of adult type and texture but does not extend onto the medial thighs. Which of the following is the most accurate Tanner stage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tanner stage 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tanner stage 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tanner stage 3

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tanner stage 4

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tanner stage 5

explanation.summary: A secondary areolar mound with adult-type pubic hair that spares the thighs defines Tanner stage 4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Tanner staging in females scores breast development and pubic hair from 1 (prepubertal) to 5 (adult). Stage 4 breast development is defined by the areola forming a secondary mound above the breast contour, and stage 4 pubic hair is adult in type but has not yet spread to the medial thighs. Both of her findings match stage 4.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Stage 1 is prepubertal, with no glandular breast tissue and no pubic hair.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Stage 2 is a breast bud with areolar enlargement and only sparse, slightly pigmented hair.
whyWrongByChoice.C: In stage 3 the breast and areola enlarge together without a separate mound, and hair is darker and curlier over the pubis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Stage 5 is the adult contour with the areola recessed back into the breast and hair reaching the medial thighs.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought in because he is the shortest child in his class. His height is at the 5th percentile and his growth velocity over the past year has been 5.5 cm. His father is 165 cm tall and his mother is 158 cm tall. He has no chronic symptoms, and physical examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for his stature?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Growth hormone deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Familial short stature

choices.label: C
choices.text: Acquired hypothyroidism

choices.label: D
choices.text: Celiac disease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Central precocious puberty

explanation.summary: A normal growth velocity with a target height that matches the child's percentile points to familial short stature.
explanation.whyCorrect: His target height from mid-parental height is (165 + 158 + 13) divided by 2, or about 168 cm, so he is tracking within his inherited genetic range. Height is a polygenic trait, and mid-parental height is the single most clinically useful genetic predictor of a child's stature. A growth velocity above the 5 cm per year minimum after age 3 argues against pathology, and 10% of normal children fall outside the 5th percentile.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Growth hormone deficiency characteristically produces a growth velocity below 5 cm per year, not the normal velocity seen here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Childhood hypothyroidism causes growth arrest with a markedly delayed bone age rather than steady normal-velocity growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Celiac disease impairs growth through malabsorption and is typically accompanied by gastrointestinal symptoms and falling velocity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Precocious puberty accelerates growth velocity and causes tall stature for age, the opposite of this picture.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has no breast development and no pubic hair. She is short compared with her classmates but has grown steadily. Her bone age is read as 11 years. Her mother reports that her own menarche occurred at age 16. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

choices.label: B
choices.text: Constitutional delay of puberty

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turner syndrome (45,X)

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premature ovarian insufficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Central precocious puberty

explanation.summary: Delayed bone age plus a family history of late puberty is the classic profile of constitutional delay.
explanation.whyCorrect: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty is the most common cause of delayed puberty and is frequently familial. These children are short for their chronological age but carry a correspondingly delayed bone age, so they retain remaining growth potential and ultimately reach a normal adult height. Her three-year bone age lag and her mother's menarche at 16 fit this pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism shows low LH and FSH with a bone age that is normal or only minimally delayed.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Turner syndrome causes short stature with dysmorphic features such as a webbed neck and an elevated FSH.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Premature ovarian insufficiency produces an elevated FSH and is uncommon at this age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Precocious puberty means early rather than absent secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.stem: A neonate born at term has a birth length and weight appropriate for gestational age. Which of the following signaling systems was the principal driver of this infant's linear growth during intrauterine life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pituitary growth hormone acting directly on bone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Adrenal dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin and insulin-like growth factor signaling

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gonadal estrogen and testosterone

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulsatile hypothalamic gonadotropin-releasing hormone

explanation.summary: Fetal growth is driven by insulin and IGF signaling, with growth hormone contributing relatively little before birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each period of growth has its own dominant hormonal regulator. During intrauterine life, insulin and IGF signaling are the primary drivers of fetal growth, while growth hormone plays only a minor role until after delivery. Only after birth does pituitary GH take over by stimulating hepatic IGF-1 production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: GH becomes the dominant driver only after birth, and it acts largely indirectly through hepatic IGF-1 rather than directly on bone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: DHEAS is the product of adrenarche and drives pubic and axillary hair development, not fetal size.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gonadal sex steroids drive the adolescent growth spurt and epiphyseal fusion, not fetal growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pulsatile GnRH activates the gonadal axis at gonadarche, well after the intrauterine period.

questions.stem: A term male infant is born at the 95th percentile for weight and length. His parents, who are both of average height, ask whether his large size at birth means he will be a tall adult. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Birth size mostly reflects the fetal genome, so it does forecast adult stature

choices.label: B
choices.text: Birth size predicts adult stature more reliably than mid-parental height does

choices.label: C
choices.text: Birth size is largely set by maternal factors, so it does not forecast stature

choices.label: D
choices.text: Birth size fixes the height percentile a child settles onto by 2 years of age

choices.label: E
choices.text: Birth size forecasts adult stature once a bone age radiograph is obtained

explanation.summary: Only about 20% of birth size traces to the fetal genome, so size at birth does not forecast adult height.
explanation.whyCorrect: Birth size is roughly 20% fetal genome, 20% maternal genome, 30% maternal environmental factors such as nutrition, health, and placental function, and 30% unexplained. Because non-heritable maternal factors carry so much of the weight, size at birth does not predict adult stature. A child instead settles onto a height percentile by about 2 years of age and then tracks along it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The fetal genome accounts for only about a fifth of birth size, so it cannot dictate adult height.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mid-parental height is the most clinically useful predictor of adult stature; birth size is not.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The percentile a child establishes by age 2 reflects postnatal growth after the maternal influence recedes, not birth size.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bone age refines a height prediction from current height, but it does not turn birth size into a predictor.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is being evaluated for a growth velocity of 3 cm per year. A random growth hormone level obtained in the clinic at 10:00 AM is low. Which of the following best explains why this single measurement cannot establish growth hormone deficiency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Growth hormone circulates bound to a carrier protein that blocks the assay

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth hormone is secreted continuously, so a low value reflects assay error

choices.label: C
choices.text: Growth hormone is released only during REM sleep, so daytime levels are low

choices.label: D
choices.text: Growth hormone rises only after a meal, so it must be drawn postprandially

choices.label: E
choices.text: Growth hormone is made in the liver, so pituitary disease does not lower it

explanation.summary: GH secretion is pulsatile and sleep-dependent, so a random daytime level is uninformative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Growth hormone secretion is not continuous. Over a 24-hour period it is released during periods of REM sleep, so a sample drawn while a child is awake in clinic can be low even in a completely normal child. This is why the growth hormone axis is judged by IGF-1 and provocative testing rather than by a single random level.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Carrier-protein binding is not why a random GH level is uninterpretable; the timing of secretion is.
whyWrongByChoice.B: GH secretion is explicitly pulsatile rather than continuous, which is the basis of the problem here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: GH release is tied to sleep, not to meals.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GH comes from the anterior pituitary; it is IGF-1 that the liver produces in response to GH.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has had breast development and pubic hair since age 6 years. She is now well above the 97th percentile for height and is taller than all of her classmates. Her bone age is advanced by 3 years. If she is left untreated, which of the following is the most likely long-term outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Final adult height well above her mid-parental target height

choices.label: B
choices.text: Continued linear growth well into the third decade of life

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progressive disproportionate lengthening of the limbs

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arrest of growth velocity below 5 cm per year within the year

choices.label: E
choices.text: Final adult height below her mid-parental target height

explanation.summary: Precocious puberty makes a child tall for age at first but shortens final height by fusing the epiphyses early.
explanation.whyCorrect: Precocious puberty, defined as onset before age 8 in females and before age 9 in males, initially accelerates growth and produces tall stature for chronological age. The same sex steroids that drive that acceleration also advance skeletal maturation and cause premature epiphyseal fusion, ending linear growth early and reducing final adult height. Her advanced bone age is the marker of that lost growth potential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Early fusion of the growth plates cuts short her growing years, so she finishes shorter, not taller, than her genetic target.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sex steroids close the growth plates, and in precocious puberty they do so earlier than normal rather than later.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disproportionately long limbs are a consequence of extended delay of puberty, not of early puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Her velocity is currently accelerated; height is lost through early epiphyseal fusion rather than immediate growth arrest.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy from a food-insecure household has a growth velocity of 3 cm per year and a weight well below the 3rd percentile. Provocative testing shows a normal growth hormone response, but his serum IGF-1 is low. Which of the following best explains these findings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A pituitary lesion that has abolished growth hormone secretion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chronic undernutrition suppressing IGF-1 despite normal growth hormone

choices.label: C
choices.text: Autonomous IGF-1 production by hepatic tissue independent of GH

choices.label: D
choices.text: Premature epiphyseal fusion from excess sex steroid exposure

choices.label: E
choices.text: A SHOX gene deletion impairing growth plate function and limb length

explanation.summary: Undernutrition lowers IGF-1 in the face of normal GH, a state of GH resistance.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nutrition is the most powerful environmental determinant of growth. Chronic undernutrition suppresses IGF-1 levels even when growth hormone secretion is normal, a state known as GH resistance, and IGF-1 is the mediator that acts on growth plates to promote chondrocyte proliferation and bone elongation. His low weight-for-age and food insecurity fit this mechanism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pituitary lesion would blunt the growth hormone response to provocative testing, which was normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Autonomous excess IGF-1 would raise, not lower, his IGF-1 level and would accelerate growth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Excess sex steroid exposure advances bone age and closes the plates; it does not lower IGF-1 with normal GH.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SHOX deletion causes a skeletal growth defect with disproportion, not a low IGF-1 with a normal GH response.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is brought for a well-child visit. The pediatrician plots head circumference at every visit during the first 2 years of life. Which of the following best explains why head circumference is such a sensitive indicator at this age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Head circumference tracks limb length better than standing height does

choices.label: B
choices.text: The head is one-tenth of body length in infancy and one-quarter in adults

choices.label: C
choices.text: Head circumference is the parameter most responsive to growth hormone

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 85% of postnatal head growth occurs in the first 18 months of life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Head circumference predicts cardiovascular risk better than body mass index

explanation.summary: Head circumference is driven by brain growth, and most of that growth is complete by 18 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: Head circumference is primarily determined by brain growth, and 85% of all postnatal head growth occurs within the first 18 months of life. Because so much neurologic development is compressed into that window, serial head circumference measurements are a sensitive indicator of neurological development in infancy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Limb length is assessed by arm span and the upper-to-lower segment ratio, not by head circumference.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The proportions are reversed: the head is about one-quarter of body length in infants and one-tenth in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Head size reflects brain growth, whereas the growth hormone axis drives linear skeletal growth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Waist-to-height ratio is the better predictor of cardiovascular risk; head circumference is not used for that.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy is evaluated for tall stature. His standing height is 191 cm and his arm span is 199 cm. He has long, slender fingers and a high-arched palate. Which of the following conditions is most consistent with this pattern of body proportions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Achondroplasia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Growth hormone deficiency

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turner syndrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marfan syndrome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Familial short stature

explanation.summary: Arm span should equal height, and a span exceeding height by more than 5 cm suggests Marfan syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Arm span equals height throughout life, even in utero, so a discrepancy greater than 5 cm is clinically notable. When arm span exceeds height, as it does here by 8 cm, the pattern points toward a long-limbed condition such as Marfan syndrome. The reverse pattern, height greater than arm span, instead suggests a skeletal dysplasia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Achondroplasia shortens the limbs, producing a high upper-to-lower segment ratio and a height that exceeds arm span.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Growth hormone deficiency causes proportionate short stature with a low growth velocity, not tall stature.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Turner syndrome causes short stature, contributed to by SHOX haploinsufficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Familial short stature involves normal proportions and a height that matches the mid-parental target.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl's height has fallen from the 50th percentile to the 10th percentile over the past 2 years, although she remains within the normal range on the growth chart. Which of the following is the single most informative parameter for deciding whether her growth is abnormal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Body mass index for age

choices.label: B
choices.text: Current height percentile

choices.label: C
choices.text: Head circumference percentile

choices.label: D
choices.text: Weight-for-height percentile

choices.label: E
choices.text: Growth velocity in cm per year

explanation.summary: Growth velocity, not a single height percentile, is the most informative parameter in growth assessment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Growth velocity is the rate of height gain over time, calculated from heights taken at least 6 months apart. After age 3, a velocity below 5 cm per year is abnormal, and crossing two major percentile lines downward during the stable childhood period is a red flag even when absolute height remains within the normal range. A child growing at a normal velocity at the 3rd percentile is reassuring; this downward crossing is not.

whyWrongByChoice.A: BMI describes weight relative to height and does not measure linear growth over time.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A single height percentile tells you where she is but not where she has been; 10% of normal children fall outside the 5th percentile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Head circumference reflects brain growth and is most useful in infancy, not for linear growth at age 5.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Weight-for-height captures nutritional status rather than the rate of height gain.

questions.stem: A pair of fraternal twins, one male and one female, are followed through puberty. The girl's peak height velocity occurs at Tanner stage 2, and the boy's occurs at Tanner stage 3 to 4. As adults, the brother is about 13 cm taller than his sister. Which of the following best explains this average height difference between adult men and women?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The male spurt starts later and is greater in magnitude

choices.label: B
choices.text: The male spurt starts earlier and lasts longer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Males lack estrogen and so never fuse their epiphyses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Males have a higher childhood growth velocity before puberty

choices.label: E
choices.text: Females fail to mount a growth hormone response to sex steroids

explanation.summary: Boys grow longer before their spurt and then grow faster during it, which accounts for the roughly 13 cm difference.
explanation.whyCorrect: In females the growth spurt begins early in puberty around Tanner stage 2, peaks at about 8 to 9 cm per year, and adds roughly 25 cm to final height. In males it begins later, around Tanner stage 3 to 4, peaks at 10 to 12 cm per year, and adds about 28 cm. The later onset buys boys extra years of prepubertal growth, and the greater peak velocity adds more centimeters, together explaining the average 13 cm difference.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The male spurt begins later in puberty than the female spurt, not earlier.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Sex steroids close the epiphyses in both sexes, which is what ultimately ends linear growth in males as well.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Childhood growth before puberty is a stable GH-driven phase that does not differ enough by sex to explain the gap.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Females do amplify GH secretion in response to estrogen; that is precisely what produces their pubertal spurt.
